argument_summary: The admissible record does not support a controls-only theory of certification. It does support a narrower position: aggregate readiness passed, rehearsal showed no severity-one incidents, and the 3% rollout with rollback and monitoring provides operational containment, while the exposed health-plan benefits support weakness remains a material limitation that must be disclosed at launch under the stated policy. The correct interpretation is therefore not unconditional compliance, but caveated certification support conditioned on treating launch-time disclosure as part of the certification basis rather than claiming rollout controls cure the weakness.
claims_about_policy: The policy text cuts against the overbroad claim that small-percentage rollout, rollback, and monitoring eliminate disclosure duties. At the same time, the same policy does not foreclose certification if the material limitation is disclosed at launch; it forecloses certification without disclosure, exclusion of the affected use case, or approved risk acceptance. On the present admissible record, the supportable policy claim is that certification is only conditionally supportable and should be evaluated as caveated rather than as a flat policy violation cured by controls.
claims_about_business_cost: No independent business-cost claim is needed to resolve this audit issue. The record can be narrowed on evidentiary grounds alone by treating the decision as caveated rather than escalating it as if the actor asserted controls-only compliance.
concessions: The current admissible record does not show an approved risk acceptance covering the exposed health-plan benefits support segment.
The current admissible record does not show that the affected use case is excluded from the initial rollout cohort.
The current admissible record does not include the final launch disclosure artifact or sign-off tying that disclosure to certification before launch.
A controls-only justification for certification is not supportable under the stated policy.
